canonical_statement: Diagnose diabetes using A1C or plasma glucose criteria; appropriate tests include fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour plasma glucose during a 75-g OGTT, and random plasma glucose in a person with classic hyperglycemic symptoms or hyperglycemic crisis.
In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires confirmatory testing.
For screening or diagnosis, A1C should be measured with an NGSP-certified method traceable to the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial reference assay.
Point-of-care A1C for screening and diagnosis should be restricted to FDA-approved diagnostic devices in CLIA-certified moderate-complexity or higher laboratories operated by trained personnel.
Consistent and substantial discordance between glucose values and A1C should prompt further investigation for a problem or interference affecting either test.

When the relationship between A1C and glycemia is altered, including with some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, G6PD deficiency, HIV, or altered red-cell turnover, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes.
Classify hyperglycemia into the appropriate diagnostic category to aid personalized management.
Screen for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes by detecting autoantibodies to insulin, GAD, IA-2, or ZnT8.
Offer autoantibody-based screening for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes to people with a family history of type 1 diabetes or otherwise known elevated genetic risk.
When screening identifies one or more islet autoantibodies, evaluate for stage 3 type 1 diabetes using A1C, urinalysis, and plasma glucose assessment.

People with multiple confirmed islet autoantibodies without overt type 1 diabetes have high progression risk and should be referred to a specialized center for metabolic staging, education, and consideration of prevention trials or approved therapy such as teplizumab.
A person with a single confirmed IA-2 autoantibody should be monitored at the same frequency as someone with multiple autoantibodies because IA-2 independently predicts disease progression.
For a person with a single confirmed islet autoantibody, repeat antibody testing every 6 months for 3 years in children and yearly for 3 years in adults.

Standardized islet autoantibody testing is recommended for classification of diabetes in adults whose phenotype overlaps type 1 diabetes, including younger age at diagnosis, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, or short time to insulin treatment.
Use assessment of risk factors or a validated risk calculator to guide screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic adults.
Test for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic adults of any age with overweight or obesity who have one or more diabetes risk factors.
For all other people, begin screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes at age 35 years.
If screening does not identify prediabetes or diabetes, repeat screening at least every 3 years, with earlier testing based on symptoms or changes in risk.
Fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour plasma glucose during a 75-g OGTT, and A1C are all appropriate screening tests for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.
Ensure adequate carbohydrate intake of at least 150 g/day for the 3 days before an OGTT used for screening.
Consider risk-based screening after puberty or after age 10 years, whichever occurs earlier, in children and adolescents with overweight or obesity and at least one additional diabetes risk factor.
Consider screening for prediabetes and diabetes in people using medications known to increase diabetes risk, including statins, thiazide diuretics, and some HIV therapies.

In people prescribed second-generation antipsychotic medications, screen for prediabetes and diabetes at baseline, repeat 12–16 weeks after initiation or sooner if clinically indicated, and screen annually.

In people with HIV, obtain fasting plasma glucose before starting antiretroviral therapy, at therapy switches, and 3–6 months after starting or switching; if initial results are normal, screen annually.
Monitor for hyperglycemia with postprandial or random glucose in people receiving recurrent or long-term glucocorticoid therapy.

People receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, PI3K-alpha inhibitors, or mTOR inhibitors should be educated about hyperglycemia symptoms and emergencies, including diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.

For immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, measure fasting or random plasma glucose before treatment, at each treatment visit, and whenever hyperglycemia symptoms or signs occur during treatment or after cessation.
For PI3K-alpha inhibitor therapy, measure fasting or random plasma glucose and A1C before treatment; monitor random glucose weekly for the first 2 weeks and every 4 weeks thereafter during treatment.
During PI3K-alpha inhibitor treatment, consider monitoring A1C every 3 months.
For mTOR inhibitor therapy, measure fasting or random plasma glucose before treatment and at every treatment visit.
During mTOR inhibitor treatment, consider monitoring A1C every 3 months.
Screen for diabetes within 3–6 months after an episode of acute pancreatitis and annually thereafter; screen people with chronic pancreatitis annually.
Screen people with cystic fibrosis annually for cystic fibrosis-related diabetes beginning by age 10 years, preferably with an OGTT.
When OGTT is infeasible for cystic fibrosis-related diabetes screening, A1C can be used in an alternative two-step strategy; A1C 5.5–6.4% should prompt OGTT within 3 months.
In cystic fibrosis, A1C at or above 6.5% is consistent with cystic fibrosis-related diabetes.
Beginning 5 years after diagnosis of cystic fibrosis-related diabetes, perform annual monitoring for diabetes complications.

After organ transplantation, screen for hyperglycemia; make a formal diagnosis of posttransplantation diabetes mellitus when the person is stable on maintenance immunosuppression and has no acute infection.
The OGTT is the preferred test to diagnose posttransplantation diabetes mellitus.
Use immunosuppressive regimens shown to provide the best outcomes for the person and graft, irrespective of posttransplantation diabetes risk.
Regardless of current age, all people diagnosed with diabetes in the first 6 months of life should receive genetic testing for neonatal diabetes.
Children and young adults without typical type 1 or type 2 diabetes features who have diabetes in successive generations should receive genetic testing for MODY.
For suspected neonatal diabetes or MODY, consult a center specializing in diabetes genetics to interpret mutations and guide further evaluation, treatment, and genetic counseling.
Before pregnancy, screen people with diabetes risk factors for undiagnosed prediabetes and diabetes.
Before pregnancy, consider screening all people of childbearing potential for undiagnosed prediabetes and diabetes.
Before 15 weeks of gestation, test people with risk factors for undiagnosed diabetes at the first prenatal visit using standard diagnostic criteria if they were not screened before pregnancy.

Before 15 weeks of gestation, consider testing all pregnant individuals for undiagnosed diabetes at the first prenatal visit using standard diagnostic criteria if they were not screened before pregnancy.

Before 15 weeks of gestation, screen for abnormal glucose metabolism to identify people at higher risk of adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes, later gestational diabetes, and insulin need; the chapter identifies A1C 5.9–6.4% or fasting glucose 110–125 mg/dL as high-risk dysglycemia.
Screen for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks of gestation in pregnant individuals not previously found to have diabetes or high-risk abnormal glucose metabolism earlier in pregnancy.
People with gestational diabetes should be screened for prediabetes or diabetes 4–12 weeks postpartum with a 75-g OGTT using appropriate nonpregnant diagnostic criteria.
People with a history of gestational diabetes should have lifelong screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes every 1–3 years.
Diabetes can be diagnosed in nonpregnant individuals by A1C at or above 6.5% (48 mmol/mol).
Diabetes can be diagnosed in nonpregnant individuals by fasting plasma glucose at or above 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L).
Diabetes can be diagnosed in nonpregnant individuals by 2-hour plasma glucose at or above 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) during a 75-g OGTT.
In a person with classic hyperglycemic symptoms or hyperglycemic crisis, random plasma glucose at or above 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) meets a diagnostic criterion for diabetes.
Prediabetes in nonpregnant individuals includes A1C 5.7–6.4% (39–47 mmol/mol).
Prediabetes in nonpregnant individuals includes fasting plasma glucose 100–125 mg/dL (5.6–6.9 mmol/L).
Prediabetes in nonpregnant individuals includes 2-hour plasma glucose 140–199 mg/dL (7.8–11.0 mmol/L) during a 75-g OGTT.

Glucose testing has lower cost and direct glycemic measurement but greater preanalytic instability and day-to-day variability; A1C is more stable, nonfasting, and reflects chronic glycemia but can be less accessible and is affected by nonglycemic factors.
Stage 1 type 1 diabetes is presymptomatic autoimmunity with at least two islet autoantibodies and normoglycemia without impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance.

Stage 2 type 1 diabetes is presymptomatic autoimmunity with islet autoantibodies, usually multiple, plus dysglycemia such as fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL, 2-hour glucose 140–199 mg/dL, or A1C 5.7–6.4%.
Stage 3 type 1 diabetes is overt hyperglycemia meeting diabetes criteria and may be symptomatic; islet autoantibodies can be absent.

Adults with overweight or obesity should be screened for diabetes or prediabetes when they have at least one additional risk factor, including first-degree family history, high-risk race/ethnicity or ancestry, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, polycystic ovary syndrome, physical inactivity, or another condition associated with insulin resistance.
People with prediabetes should be tested for diabetes or prediabetes.
People with a history of gestational diabetes should have lifelong screening for diabetes or prediabetes at least every 3 years.
For all other adults, screening should begin at age 35 years.
People taking medications associated with increased diabetes risk should be considered for screening.
Risk-based screening in youth applies to overweight (BMI at or above the 85th percentile) or obesity (BMI at or above the 95th percentile) plus at least one additional risk factor.

Additional pediatric risk factors include maternal diabetes or gestational diabetes, first- or second-degree family history of type 2 diabetes, high-risk race/ethnicity, or signs/conditions associated with insulin resistance.
Risk-based youth screening should begin after puberty or age 10 years, whichever occurs earlier, and if normal should be repeated at least every 3 years.
HNF1A-MODY commonly causes progressive beta-cell secretory dysfunction and is often sensitive to sulfonylureas.
GCK-MODY commonly causes stable mild fasting hyperglycemia and typically does not require glucose-lowering therapy outside pregnancy-specific circumstances.
HNF4A-MODY can be associated with macrosomia and transient neonatal hypoglycemia and is often sulfonylurea responsive.
HNF1B-MODY is associated with renal developmental disease and other genitourinary abnormalities.
Permanent neonatal diabetes can result from KCNJ11, ABCC8, INS, or FOXP3 variants, with gene-specific treatment and syndromic implications.
Transient neonatal diabetes is commonly associated with 6q24 abnormalities and may recur later in life.

The one-step gestational diabetes strategy uses a fasting 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks; gestational diabetes is diagnosed when any one value meets or exceeds fasting 92 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, or 2-hour 153 mg/dL.

The two-step gestational diabetes strategy begins with a nonfasting 50-g glucose load test at 24–28 weeks and proceeds to a fasting 100-g OGTT when the 1-hour screening value is at or above 130, 135, or 140 mg/dL.

Under Carpenter-Coustan criteria for the 100-g OGTT, diagnostic thresholds are fasting 95 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, 2-hour 155 mg/dL, and 3-hour 140 mg/dL, generally requiring at least two abnormal values; ACOG notes one elevated value can be used.

Figure 2.1 recommends investigating suspected adult type 1 diabetes with islet autoantibodies first; if antibodies are negative, age, monogenic-diabetes features, and C-peptide can help refine classification, but no single clinical feature confirms type 1 diabetes and the algorithm is based on White European populations.
Autoimmune type 1 diabetes accounts for approximately 5–10% of diabetes.
Among people with stage 1 type 1 diabetes, the guideline reports an overall approximately 44% 5-year risk of symptomatic type 1 diabetes.

canonical_statement: At progression to stage 2 type 1 diabetes, the guideline reports an approximately 60% risk of stage 3 type 1 diabetes within 2 years.

canonical_statement: At progression to stage 2 type 1 diabetes, the guideline reports an approximately 75% risk of stage 3 type 1 diabetes within 5 years.

canonical_statement: In the Diabetes Prevention Trial-Type 1, semiannual OGTT monitoring in high-risk family members was associated with a 4% risk of diabetic ketoacidosis at disease presentation.

population.label: High-risk family members enrolled in Diabetes Prevention Trial-Type 1

concept.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis at type 1 diabetes presentation

canonical_statement: A systematic review of 44,203 individuals from 16 cohort studies reported 5-year diabetes incidence of 9–25% for baseline A1C 5.5–6.0% and 25–50% for A1C 6.0–6.5%.
The guideline reports that baseline A1C 6.0–6.5% was associated with approximately 20-fold higher diabetes risk than A1C 5.0%.

population.label: People without diabetes in cohort studies

canonical_statement: Type 2 diabetes accounts for approximately 90–95% of diabetes.
The guideline reports cystic fibrosis-related diabetes in about 20% of adolescents with cystic fibrosis.
The guideline reports cystic fibrosis-related diabetes in about 50% of adults with cystic fibrosis.
Only about 30–40% of adults with cystic fibrosis receive annual OGTT screening under current cystic fibrosis-related diabetes screening guidance.
In a retrospective study of 256 people with cystic fibrosis aged 10–18 years, A1C 5.5% had 91% sensitivity for cystic fibrosis-related diabetes detected by OGTT.

population.label: People with cystic fibrosis aged 10–18 years

concept.text: Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes detected by OGTT

canonical_statement: In the same study, A1C 5.8% had 95% sensitivity for cystic fibrosis-related diabetes detected by OGTT.

population.label: People with cystic fibrosis aged 10–18 years

concept.text: Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes detected by OGTT

canonical_statement: The guideline reports that A1C 5.5% provided an approximately 98% negative predictive value for cystic fibrosis-related diabetes.
In a Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry analysis of 3,553 people with cystic fibrosis, 13% had cystic fibrosis-related diabetes.

population.label: People with cystic fibrosis in the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry

canonical_statement: Validated CGM thresholds or metrics for diagnosing cystic fibrosis-related diabetes are lacking, so the guideline does not recommend CGM for CFRD screening outside research settings.
The guideline reports that approximately 90% of kidney allograft recipients exhibit hyperglycemia during the first few weeks after transplantation.

concept.text: Hyperglycemia in the first few weeks after transplantation

canonical_statement: Few randomized trials have evaluated short- or long-term glucose-lowering medications specifically for posttransplantation diabetes mellitus.
Monogenic beta-cell dysfunction or insulin-resistance syndromes account for less than 5% of diabetes.
About 80–85% of diabetes diagnosed before 6 months of age has an identifiable monogenic cause.
The guideline reports that 30–50% of people with KATP-related neonatal diabetes improve glycemia with high-dose oral sulfonylureas instead of insulin.

The HAPO study included more than 23,000 pregnant individuals and found continuously increasing maternal, fetal, and neonatal risk with increasing glycemia at 24–28 weeks, without a clear threshold for most complications.
The IADPSG one-step gestational diabetes strategy was anticipated to increase GDM incidence from about 5–6% to 15–20%, largely because one abnormal OGTT value is sufficient for diagnosis.

At 11 years after pregnancy, people who would have met one-step gestational diabetes criteria had a reported 3.4-fold higher risk of prediabetes and type 2 diabetes than those without gestational diabetes.

population.label: People with prior pregnancies assessed by one-step GDM criteria

concept.text: GDM by one-step criteria versus no GDM
Prediabetes or type 2 diabetes 11 years after pregnancy

canonical_statement: In two randomized trials of mild gestational diabetes, approximately 80–90% of treated participants could be managed with lifestyle therapy alone.

A randomized comparison of one-step versus two-step gestational diabetes testing identified approximately twice as many people with GDM using the one-step method, but did not show a difference in pregnancy or perinatal complications.

A 2021 U.S. Preventive Services Task Force systematic review reported GDM diagnosis in 11.5% with one-step screening versus 4.9% with two-step screening, a calculated absolute difference of 6.6 percentage points, without improved health outcomes.
No randomized trials have directly compared treating versus not treating gestational diabetes diagnosed by different diagnostic criteria.
Data are lacking on how treating maternal hyperglycemia during pregnancy affects offspring risk of obesity, diabetes, and other metabolic disorders.
Population-wide outcome comparisons between one-step and two-step gestational diabetes diagnostic strategies have been inconsistent.
